q: A developer uses GitHub Copilot to generate a function. Before merging, what is the most important step according to responsible AI principles?
opts: Accept the suggestion immediately to save time
Review and validate the AI-generated code before committing
Reject all AI suggestions to maintain code ownership
Share the suggestion with the team for a vote
exp: Responsible AI use requires that humans always review and validate AI output. AI should never have the final say without human oversight.

q: Which two of the following are key principles of responsible AI use with GitHub Copilot? (Select 2)
opts: Fairness — ensuring AI does not reinforce existing biases
Speed — always prioritising the fastest suggestion
Transparency — being clear about how AI decisions are made
Automation — letting AI make final decisions autonomously
exp: Fairness and transparency are two of the core responsible AI pillars. 'Automation without oversight' and pure speed are not responsible AI principles.

q: Which phrase best describes a key limitation of GitHub Copilot that developers must account for?
opts: It can only generate code in JavaScript and Python
It may produce plausible-looking but incorrect or insecure code
It always references the latest security patches
It requires an internet connection to generate all suggestions
exp: Copilot can generate code that looks correct but contains bugs or security vulnerabilities. Developers must validate output.

q: A Copilot suggestion subtly reinforces a biased outcome in a classification model. Which responsible AI principle is most directly at stake?
opts: Transparency
Security
Fairness
Accountability
exp: Fairness addresses whether AI outputs perpetuate or amplify biases. The exam often tests the distinction between fairness and inclusion.

q: Which of the following best describes 'accountability' in responsible AI use with GitHub Copilot?
opts: GitHub automatically logs all accepted suggestions for legal review
Developers take responsibility for reviewing, testing, and owning AI-generated code they commit
AI models are held legally responsible for bugs in generated code
Organisations must publish all Copilot usage publicly
exp: Accountability means the developer who accepts and commits AI-generated code owns it — both legally and professionally.

q: Which two strategies help mitigate the risks of AI-generated code in a production codebase? (Select 2)
opts: Always run AI-generated code through automated tests and code review
Disable linting tools so Copilot suggestions appear faster
Apply security scanning to catch potential vulnerabilities in suggestions
Trust Copilot to handle edge cases without manual verification
exp: Running tests/code review and applying security scanning are concrete mitigation strategies. Disabling linting and skipping verification increase risk.

q: A developer notices Copilot consistently suggests code that uses deprecated APIs. What is the responsible course of action?
opts: Accept the suggestions anyway since Copilot is usually right
Validate and update the suggestions to use current APIs before committing
Disable Copilot permanently for the project
Report the issue and wait for GitHub to fix the model
exp: Developers are responsible for validating AI output. Suggestions referencing outdated APIs should be updated before committing — this is a core human-in-the-loop responsibility.

q: What does 'transparency' mean in the context of responsible AI use with GitHub Copilot?
opts: GitHub publishes the source code of the AI model
Developers disclose when AI was used to generate code in their team's workflow
Copilot shows the exact training data used for each suggestion
All suggestions are logged and available publicly
exp: Transparency in responsible AI means being open about how AI tools are used in development processes — e.g. disclosing AI assistance to teammates or reviewers.

q: Which of the following is a potential harm of over-relying on GitHub Copilot without human review?
opts: Suggestions will always be syntactically correct
Developers may introduce security vulnerabilities without realising it
AI will automatically refactor the entire codebase
Copilot will start rejecting suggestions after overuse
exp: Over-reliance without review risks introducing bugs, security holes, or biased logic that the developer would otherwise catch.

q: How does GitHub Copilot address the risk of generating harmful or offensive content in code comments or strings?
opts: It requires manual content review by GitHub staff before showing suggestions
It applies a toxicity filter as part of its prompt processing pipeline
It blocks all natural-language content and only generates code
It relies entirely on the developer's judgement with no automated safeguard
exp: GitHub Copilot's proxy pipeline includes a toxicity filter that screens both input and output for harmful content before suggestions are displayed.

q: A company wants to prevent developer code from being used to train GitHub Copilot's AI models. Which plan is the minimum required?
opts: GitHub Copilot Free
GitHub Copilot Pro
GitHub Copilot Business
GitHub Copilot Individual
exp: Business and Enterprise plans include the policy that user prompts are not retained or used for model training. Free and Pro plans do not guarantee this at an organisational level.

q: An enterprise wants centralised policy management, audit log access, and content exclusion enforcement across all repositories. Which plan supports all of these?
opts: GitHub Copilot Pro
GitHub Copilot Free
GitHub Copilot Business
GitHub Copilot Individual
exp: Business (and Enterprise) plans include organisation-level policy management, audit logs, and content exclusion enforcement.

q: Which two features are available in GitHub Copilot Enterprise but NOT in GitHub Copilot Business? (Select 2)
opts: Organisation-wide content exclusions
Copilot Chat on github.com with context of the organisation's codebase
Fine-tuned models customised on your organisation's private code
Duplication detection / public code matching toggle
exp: Enterprise adds Copilot Chat on github.com with org-wide context awareness, and fine-tuned models on private code. Business already includes content exclusions and duplication detection.

q: A developer asks: 'How can I ensure suggestions generated for me are never used to improve Copilot's models for other users?' What is the correct answer?
opts: Enable the duplication filter in IDE settings
Switch to GitHub Copilot Business or Enterprise
Disable telemetry in the IDE extension
Add a .copilotignore file to the repository
exp: Opting out of training data collection is a Business/Enterprise plan policy enforced organisation-wide. IDE-level settings do not control this.

q: A startup with 10 developers uses GitHub Copilot Business. They now need Copilot to answer questions using context from their internal wiki and private codebase on github.com. What should they do?
opts: Upgrade to GitHub Copilot Enterprise
Enable the knowledge base feature in Business settings
Add a copilot-instructions.md to each repository
Use GitHub Actions to sync context to Copilot
exp: Enterprise adds the ability to index private repositories and internal content for use in Copilot Chat on github.com. This is not available in Business.

q: Which plan allows an organisation to manage Copilot subscriptions using the REST API?
opts: Copilot Free only
Copilot Pro only
Copilot Business and Enterprise
All plans including Free
exp: The REST API for managing Copilot seats and subscriptions is available for Business and Enterprise plan administrators.

q: A CTO asks: 'Under which Copilot plan can we enforce that developers may only use Copilot in approved IDEs?' What is the correct answer?
opts: This cannot be enforced on any plan
GitHub Copilot Free
GitHub Copilot Pro
GitHub Copilot Business or Enterprise
exp: Organisation-level feature availability controls (including restricting which IDEs can use Copilot) are available only on Business and Enterprise plans.

q: Which two scenarios would require upgrading from Copilot Business to Copilot Enterprise? (Select 2)
opts: The organisation wants Copilot Chat on github.com to reference private repository context
The organisation wants to enforce content exclusions org-wide
The organisation wants to customise the AI model on their own codebase
The organisation wants to enable the public code matching filter
exp: Enterprise-only features are: Copilot Chat on github.com with private context awareness, and fine-tuning the model on private code. Content exclusions and public code matching are Business features.

q: A developer wants to ensure their code contributed to an open-source project is never stored by GitHub for AI training. Which plan feature addresses this?
opts: Free plan telemetry opt-out per user
Business/Enterprise plan data retention policy
Pro plan incognito mode
Individual plan privacy toggle in IDE
exp: Data retention and training exclusion policies are enforced at the organisation level under Business/Enterprise. Individual opt-outs via IDE settings are unreliable for this guarantee.

q: What is the key difference between the Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise audit log capabilities?
opts: Business has no audit log; Enterprise does
Enterprise audit logs include Copilot Chat on github.com activity; Business logs are limited to IDE events
Business and Enterprise have identical audit logs
Enterprise retains logs for 7 days; Business retains for 180 days
exp: Enterprise extends audit log coverage to include Copilot Chat interactions on github.com, in addition to IDE-level events available in Business.

q: A developer adds exclusion rules in their repository's .github folder. What is the scope?
opts: Applies to all repositories in the organisation
Applies only to the repository where the file exists
Applies globally to the developer's IDE
Applies to all repositories owned by the same user
exp: Repository-level exclusion rules are scoped to that single repository only. Org-wide rules must be set in Organisation settings.

q: If a path is excluded at the Organisation level, and a developer's repository does NOT exclude that path, what happens?
opts: The repository setting overrides the organisation setting
The path remains excluded — exclusions are additive
The developer can override it locally in the IDE
It depends on the user's plan tier
exp: Exclusions are additive: if a path is excluded at any level, it remains excluded. A lower level cannot un-exclude what a higher level has blocked.

q: Which two statements about content exclusions in GitHub Copilot are correct? (Select 2)
opts: Organisation-level exclusions apply to all repositories in that organisation
A repository-level exclusion overrides an organisation-level exclusion
Exclusions are additive — exclusion at any level persists
A developer can re-include org-excluded files using local IDE settings
exp: Org exclusions propagate to all repos in the org. Exclusions are additive — lower levels cannot override higher-level blocks.

q: Where should an admin define exclusion rules to ensure they apply across every repository in an organisation?
opts: In each repository's .github folder
In the Organisation-level GitHub Copilot settings
In each developer's IDE configuration
In the Enterprise policy dashboard only
exp: Organisation-level GitHub Copilot settings is the correct place for rules that must apply organisation-wide.

q: A team defines a content exclusion at the local IDE level. Which statement is true?
opts: It applies to all users in the organisation
It applies only within that developer's IDE session for that path
It overrides repository-level exclusions
It is synced to the organisation's exclusion list automatically
exp: IDE-level exclusions apply only to that developer's local context. They do not affect other users and cannot override higher-level exclusions.

q: What effect does a content exclusion have on GitHub Copilot when a matching file is open?
opts: Copilot generates suggestions but marks them as excluded
Copilot is disabled entirely for the whole project
Copilot will not use the excluded file as context and will not suggest completions within it
The file is deleted from the repository
exp: Excluded files are ignored as context and receive no inline suggestions. Copilot does not use them to inform completions in other files either.

q: An organisation wants to prevent Copilot from suggesting code based on a proprietary algorithm file. What is the correct approach?
opts: Add the file to .gitignore
Define a content exclusion for that file path in Organisation-level Copilot settings
Encrypt the file so Copilot cannot read it
Set the file as read-only in the OS
exp: Content exclusions in Organisation-level Copilot settings are the correct mechanism to prevent specific files from being used as context or receiving suggestions.

q: A content exclusion is defined at both the repository level and the IDE level for the same path. Which two statements are true? (Select 2)
opts: The IDE-level exclusion is ignored since repository takes precedence
Both exclusions apply — the path is excluded in both contexts
If a third-level (org) exclusion is absent, the path is only excluded locally for that developer
Exclusions from all levels combine — the path remains excluded regardless of which level defines it
exp: Exclusions are additive across all levels. When a path is excluded at any level, it stays excluded. Multiple levels defining the same exclusion simply reinforce each other.

q: How long does GitHub retain Copilot audit log events for Business plan organisations by default?
opts: 7 days
30 days
90 days
180 days
exp: GitHub retains audit log events for 180 days for Business/Enterprise organisations. This specific retention period is frequently tested.

q: Which two of the following actions are captured in the GitHub Copilot audit log? (Select 2)
opts: A user enabling GitHub Copilot for their account
The exact code suggestions that were accepted by a developer
An admin changing the duplication detection policy
A developer's local IDE configuration changes
exp: Audit logs capture account/policy-level events. They do NOT record the content of specific code suggestions or local IDE settings.

q: An organisation wants to monitor which members are actively using GitHub Copilot and how frequently. Which tool should they use?
opts: The GitHub Copilot audit log
GitHub Copilot usage metrics in organisation settings
The repository's git commit history
GitHub Actions workflow logs
exp: Usage metrics show seat usage and activity per member. Audit logs record policy/administrative events, not usage frequency.

q: An admin wants to know when a specific developer's Copilot seat was assigned. Where is this information found?
opts: The developer's personal GitHub settings
The organisation audit log
The repository's blame view
The Copilot Chat history
exp: Seat assignment events are recorded in the organisation audit log, which captures administrative actions like adding or removing Copilot access for members.

q: What data is NOT available in the GitHub Copilot usage metrics dashboard?
opts: Number of suggestions accepted per developer
Number of active Copilot seats
The specific code content of accepted suggestions
Acceptance rate trends over time
exp: Usage metrics show aggregate statistics (counts, rates, active seats). The actual code content of suggestions is never stored or displayed in dashboards.

q: For how long does GitHub retain prompts and suggestions from GitHub Copilot for Business by default?
opts: Prompts are retained for 28 days for abuse detection
Prompts are not retained after the suggestion is returned — they are discarded
Prompts are stored indefinitely for model improvement
Prompts are stored for 90 days and then anonymised
exp: For Business/Enterprise, prompts are not retained after the API call completes. They are used only to generate the suggestion and are then discarded.

q: What does the GitHub Copilot duplication filter (public code matching) do when enabled?
opts: Blocks suggestions that match publicly known security vulnerabilities
Suppresses code suggestions that closely match code found in public repositories
Prevents users from copying code from public GitHub repos
Scans your repo for duplicated functions
exp: The duplication filter suppresses suggestions that closely match publicly available code on GitHub, to reduce potential licence or IP concerns.

q: At which level can a Business plan administrator configure the public code matching (duplication) filter?
opts: Only at the repository level via .copilotignore
Only at each developer's IDE settings
At the organisation level in Copilot policy settings
At the enterprise level only
exp: Business plan admins configure public code matching at the organisation level. Individual users cannot override this if set by the org.

q: A developer working under a Business plan organisation has the duplication filter disabled in their IDE, but the organisation policy has it enabled. What happens?
opts: The developer's IDE setting takes precedence — filter is disabled
The organisation setting takes precedence — filter is enabled
Both settings apply simultaneously, causing a conflict error
The filter state is undefined until the next policy sync
exp: Organisation-level policies override individual IDE settings. This is consistent with the cascade logic: a lower level cannot override a higher-level policy.

q: What context does the duplication filter use to determine if a suggestion matches public code?
opts: The exact filename and directory structure
A semantic comparison of the suggested code block against public GitHub repositories
The developer's commit history
The repository's language settings
exp: The filter compares generated suggestions against an index of public code on GitHub to detect near-matches before surfacing the suggestion.

q: A developer provides three examples of input-output pairs before asking Copilot to generate a function. Which prompting technique is this?
opts: Zero-shot prompting
One-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
Role prompting
exp: Few-shot prompting provides multiple examples (typically 2+) to guide the model. One-shot = 1 example; zero-shot = no examples.

q: A developer starts their Copilot Chat message with 'You are a senior security engineer reviewing this code for vulnerabilities.' What technique is this?
opts: Few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Role prompting
Chain-of-thought prompting
exp: Role prompting assigns a persona to the model to influence the style, expertise level, and perspective of its response.

q: Which statement best describes 'context' in GitHub Copilot's prompt processing?
opts: Only the text in the current file being edited
The current file, open tabs, chat history, and other signals used to build the prompt
Only the last message in the Copilot Chat window
The repository's README and configuration files only
exp: Context includes the active file, open/recent tabs, chat history, referenced files, and other signals Copilot uses to construct the actual prompt sent to the model.

q: Which two practices are considered best for crafting effective Copilot prompts? (Select 2)
opts: Provide specific, detailed instructions with examples where possible
Always keep prompts as short as possible (one word)
Include relevant context such as function signatures or existing code
Rely on Copilot to infer intent without any guidance
exp: Specificity and providing context (signatures, examples, related code) are best practices. Vague or minimal prompts reduce suggestion quality.

q: A developer asks Copilot to generate a function without providing any examples or context. Which prompting technique is this?
opts: Zero-shot prompting
One-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
Role prompting
exp: Zero-shot prompting provides no examples — the model relies entirely on the instruction and its training. It often produces less targeted results than one-shot or few-shot.

q: Why is chat history important in GitHub Copilot Chat sessions?
opts: It is stored permanently and used to train the model
It provides ongoing context helping Copilot give more relevant follow-up responses within the session
It is shared across all users in the organisation
It replaces the need for file context
exp: Chat history is included as context in subsequent turns of a session, helping Copilot maintain coherence. It is session-scoped and not shared or persistent.

q: What is the benefit of including a specific function signature in a Copilot prompt?
opts: It forces Copilot to use a specific programming language
It provides structural context that guides Copilot to generate a compatible, well-typed implementation
It disables Copilot's fallback suggestions
It limits the token count of the response
exp: Including a function signature gives Copilot concrete structural context — parameter types, return type, naming conventions — leading to more accurate implementations.

q: A developer provides one example input-output pair before asking Copilot to generate similar code. What technique is being used?
opts: Zero-shot prompting
One-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
System prompting
exp: One-shot prompting provides exactly one example to guide the model. It is more targeted than zero-shot but less guided than few-shot.

q: How does GitHub Copilot determine which files and code to include in the context sent to the model?
opts: It includes every file in the repository alphabetically
It uses signals like open tabs, the active file, recent edits, and imported files to select the most relevant context
It only uses the file currently open in the editor
It requires the developer to manually pin files as context
exp: Copilot uses intelligent context selection based on relevance signals: open tabs, the current file, edit history, and imports — not simply all files.

q: When a developer sends a prompt to GitHub Copilot, where is the proxy server that processes the request located?
opts: On the developer's local machine
At GitHub's servers — between the IDE and the AI model
Inside the IDE extension itself
On the organisation's private cloud infrastructure
exp: GitHub runs a proxy server that sits between the IDE and the LLM. It handles filtering, telemetry, and policy enforcement.

q: What is the purpose of the toxicity filter in GitHub Copilot's processing pipeline?
opts: It removes duplicate code from suggestions
It filters out prompts or suggestions containing harmful, offensive, or unsafe content
It blocks code that matches public licences
It prevents credentials from appearing in suggestions
exp: The toxicity filter screens both input prompts and output suggestions for harmful or inappropriate content as part of the responsible AI pipeline.

q: What does GitHub Copilot's post-processing step do after the model returns a suggestion?
opts: It sends the suggestion directly to the repository
It applies additional filtering (toxicity, duplication, security) before showing the suggestion to the developer
It commits the code to the current branch
It emails the suggestion to the organisation admin
exp: Post-processing applies further filters to raw model output before the suggestion is shown in the IDE.

q: What does it mean when GitHub Copilot documentation refers to 'proxy filtering'?
opts: Filtering code through a VPN before reaching GitHub
Pre- and post-processing of prompts and responses by GitHub's server layer to enforce safety and policy rules
Blocking all traffic from outside the organisation's network
Encrypting suggestions before they are shown in the IDE
exp: Proxy filtering refers to GitHub's server-side layer applying toxicity, duplication, and policy checks both before prompts reach the LLM and after the model responds.

q: Which of the following best describes a Large Language Model (LLM) as used by GitHub Copilot?
opts: A traditional rule-based search engine for code patterns
A neural network trained on large amounts of text and code that generates predictions based on input context
A database of pre-approved code snippets
A compiler that checks code correctness
exp: An LLM is a neural network trained on large corpora of text/code. It generates probabilistic predictions, not rule-based lookups or pre-stored snippets.

q: Where is the GitHub Copilot proxy server located relative to the developer's workflow?
opts: Between the developer's IDE and the internet
Between the developer's IDE and the AI model, on GitHub's infrastructure
Between the AI model and GitHub's code storage
On the developer's local device as part of the IDE extension
exp: The proxy sits between the IDE client and the underlying AI model on GitHub's infrastructure. It is not local and not at the storage layer.

q: Which two processes occur in the prompt-building phase before a request is sent to the LLM? (Select 2)
opts: Relevant context is assembled from open files and editor signals
The model generates an initial suggestion for review
Toxicity and content filters are applied to the outgoing prompt
The duplication filter compares the prompt against public code
exp: Before reaching the LLM, context is assembled and outgoing prompts are checked for harmful content. The model hasn't responded yet, so suggestion generation and output-side duplication checks happen after.

q: A developer is concerned about data privacy. Under GitHub Copilot Business, which statement about prompt data is accurate?
opts: Prompts are stored for 28 days for debugging
Prompts are sent to a third-party AI provider and retained indefinitely
Prompts are not retained after the suggestion is returned; they are discarded
Prompts are encrypted and stored in the organisation's private cloud
exp: For Business/Enterprise, prompts are not retained post-response. They are used only to generate the suggestion, then discarded — this is a key data handling guarantee.

q: Which interaction mode should a developer use for quick, conversational questions about a specific piece of code without modifying files?
opts: Agent mode
Edit mode
Ask mode
Plan mode
exp: Ask mode is for conversational queries. Edit mode targets specific code changes; Plan mode creates multi-step strategies; Agent mode handles autonomous multi-file execution.

q: A developer needs to refactor a feature spanning 12 files with coordinated changes across the codebase. Which mode is most appropriate?
opts: Ask mode
Edit mode
Plan mode
Agent mode
exp: Agent mode provides autonomous reasoning and execution across multiple files for complex, multi-file tasks.

q: What is the key distinction between Plan mode and Agent mode?
opts: Plan mode generates code; Agent mode only explains it
Plan mode creates structured multi-step strategies for human review; Agent mode autonomously executes code changes
Plan mode works only in VS Code; Agent mode works in all IDEs
Plan mode requires an Enterprise licence; Agent mode is available on all plans
exp: Plan mode produces a strategy for the developer to review before any changes. Agent mode goes further and can autonomously write, edit, and apply changes across files.

q: What is the purpose of a `.github/copilot-instructions.md` file?
opts: It lists files Copilot should exclude from suggestions
It provides custom instructions to Copilot Chat for all interactions in that repository
It configures the Copilot licence for the repository
It defines which IDE extensions are allowed
exp: copilot-instructions.md lets teams embed custom context — coding standards, conventions, domain knowledge — that Copilot Chat uses for all interactions in the repository.

q: What is GitHub Copilot's Pull Request Summaries feature?
opts: A tool that automatically merges approved PRs
An AI-generated description of the changes, context, and potential impact of a pull request
A report of all Copilot suggestions accepted during a PR
A code review checklist generated per repository
exp: PR Summaries uses AI to draft a natural language description of what changed and why, helping reviewers understand pull requests more quickly.

q: What are MCP servers in the context of GitHub Copilot Agent mode?
opts: Managed Cloud Providers that host Copilot's AI model
Model Context Protocol servers that extend Agent mode with external tools and data sources
Security servers that scan Copilot suggestions for malware
Monitoring servers that track developer productivity
exp: MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers allow Agent mode to connect to external tools and data sources, extending what the agent can do beyond the local codebase.

q: What is GitHub Spark?
opts: A performance profiling tool for Copilot suggestions
An AI-powered tool for building small web apps using natural language
A GitHub Actions workflow that runs Copilot in CI/CD pipelines
A plugin for integrating Copilot with Slack
exp: GitHub Spark lets users describe an application in natural language and have AI generate and deploy a simple web app — targeting non-developers or rapid prototyping.

q: What is GitHub Copilot Spaces?
opts: A cloud storage feature for code snippets
A collaborative workspace where teams can share Copilot context and instructions
A container environment for running Copilot-generated code
A repository analytics dashboard
exp: Spaces is a feature that lets teams create shared Copilot environments with shared context and instructions, enabling more consistent AI-assisted collaboration.

q: Which two of the following are valid ways to trigger GitHub Copilot inline suggestions in the IDE? (Select 2)
opts: By typing code — suggestions appear automatically as you write
By pressing Alt+\\ (or Option+\\) to manually trigger a suggestion
By right-clicking and selecting 'Generate with Copilot'
By running git commit with a --copilot flag
exp: Copilot suggests inline automatically as you type, and can be manually triggered with Alt+\\ (Windows/Linux) or Option+\\ (Mac).

q: When would a developer use Edit mode instead of Ask mode in Copilot Chat?
opts: When they want a conversational explanation of a concept
When they want to make targeted code changes directly in the file
When they want to plan a complex multi-file refactoring
When they want Copilot to autonomously fix bugs across the codebase
exp: Edit mode is designed for targeted, direct code modifications — the developer specifies what to change, and Copilot makes the edit in place. Ask mode is for Q&A without file modification.

q: A developer uses Copilot for code review. What kind of feedback does Copilot provide?
opts: It automatically approves or rejects pull requests
It suggests improvements, flags potential issues, and explains code behaviour — but requires developer review of its own feedback
It runs the code in a sandbox and reports runtime errors
It generates a code review that is final and legally binding
exp: Copilot code review provides AI-generated suggestions and observations. Like all AI output, its feedback requires human review — it does not auto-approve or take final action.

q: What is the purpose of Sub-Agents in GitHub Copilot Agent mode?
opts: Sub-Agents are backup models used when the primary model is unavailable
Sub-Agents are delegated tasks within an Agent session to optimise context usage across parallel workstreams
Sub-Agents are junior developer accounts with limited Copilot access
Sub-Agents monitor token usage and alert the admin when limits are reached
exp: Sub-Agents in Agent mode allow tasks to be delegated to specialised agents within a session, helping manage context window usage and parallelise complex tasks.

q: How do prompt files (`.github/prompts/`) differ from copilot-instructions.md?
opts: Prompt files are only for CLI use; copilot-instructions.md is for the IDE
Prompt files are reusable, shareable prompt templates for specific tasks; copilot-instructions.md provides always-on repository-level context
They are identical in functionality
Prompt files override copilot-instructions.md when both are present
exp: Prompt files are task-specific, reusable templates (e.g. a 'write unit tests' prompt) that can be invoked on demand. copilot-instructions.md is always-active context for the whole repo.

q: What is the correct sequence to start using GitHub Copilot CLI for the first time after installation?
opts: gh copilot suggest then gh auth login then trust folder
gh auth login then open browser to authenticate then gh copilot start
Trust the folder, then gh auth login, then browser opens automatically, then Copilot CLI is ready
npm install then gh copilot configure then gh auth login
exp: The CLI setup sequence confirmed by multiple exam takers: trust the folder, then gh auth login, browser opens automatically for authentication, then Copilot CLI is ready.

q: Which command is used to ask GitHub Copilot CLI for help constructing a shell command?
opts: gh copilot ask
gh copilot explain
gh copilot run
gh copilot suggest
exp: 'gh copilot suggest' asks Copilot to suggest a shell command. 'gh copilot explain' explains a given command.

q: You are in a CLI session under /root/projectA and need to trust the folder /root/projectB without leaving the current session. What should you do?
opts: Exit the session, navigate to /root/projectB, then run gh copilot trust
Run gh copilot trust /root/projectB from within the current session
Open a new terminal tab and navigate to /root/projectB
Edit ~/.gitconfig to add the trusted path
exp: You can trust a different folder from within an active CLI session by providing the target path: 'gh copilot trust /root/projectB'. No need to exit.

q: What does `gh copilot explain` do?
opts: Opens GitHub Copilot Chat in the browser
Provides a natural language explanation of a given shell command
Generates a new shell script based on a description
Authenticates the CLI session with GitHub
exp: 'gh copilot explain' takes a shell command and provides a natural language explanation of what it does — useful for understanding unfamiliar commands.

q: After installing the GitHub CLI extension for Copilot, which base command is used to interact with Copilot from the terminal?
opts: copilot
github copilot
gh copilot
git copilot
exp: The correct command prefix is 'gh copilot'. The GitHub CLI uses 'gh' as the base, with 'copilot' as the extension sub-command.

q: A developer is in a Copilot CLI interactive session and wants to generate a bash script. Which command starts this process?
opts: gh copilot script
gh copilot suggest --script
gh copilot suggest
gh copilot generate
exp: 'gh copilot suggest' is the command for requesting command or script suggestions in the CLI. The type of output is selected interactively.

q: An organisation admin wants to prevent developers from using GitHub Copilot in a specific IDE. Where should this be configured?
opts: In each developer's IDE settings
In the repository's .github folder
In the Organisation-level Copilot policy settings under feature availability
In the Enterprise GitHub dashboard only
exp: Organisation-level Copilot policy settings include controls for which IDEs and surfaces Copilot features are available on.

q: What is the cascade logic for GitHub Copilot configuration levels?
opts: Individual settings always override organisation settings
A lower level can expand but never restrict what a higher level defines
A lower level can never grant permissions that a higher level has blocked
Organisation settings only apply to Enterprise plan users
exp: This is the core cascade rule: Enterprise > Organisation > Repository > Individual. A lower level cannot unlock something blocked at a higher level.

q: A new developer joins an organisation and their IDE is configured to show Copilot suggestions, but the organisation policy blocks Copilot in all IDEs. What happens?
opts: The developer's local IDE setting takes precedence
Copilot suggestions are shown but flagged as policy-violating
No suggestions are shown — the organisation policy overrides local settings
The developer is prompted to request an exception
exp: Organisation-level policies override individual/IDE-level settings. This is the cascade logic in action.

q: Which two statements correctly describe how GitHub Copilot code review policies work? (Select 2)
opts: Admins can enable Copilot as an automatic reviewer on pull requests
Copilot Code Review replaces all human reviewers
Custom review standards can be defined using instructions files
Code review policies can only be applied at the repository level, not org-wide
exp: Admins can configure Copilot as an automatic reviewer, and custom standards can be set via instructions files. Human review is still expected; policies can be applied org-wide.

q: An Enterprise admin blocks GitHub Copilot usage on github.com for all members. A Business unit admin tries to re-enable it for their team. What is the outcome?
opts: The Business unit admin can override the Enterprise policy
The Enterprise policy takes precedence — Copilot on github.com remains blocked
The setting is undefined until GitHub support intervenes
The individual user's preference determines the outcome
exp: Enterprise-level policies are the highest level and cannot be overridden by lower levels (organisation, team, individual).

Approving and merging pull requests automatically

Content exclusion configuration

Sample data generation
Content exclusion
Pull Request summarisation

It generates certificates of completion for coding tasks
It automatically promotes junior developers to senior roles

Tests are always syntactically incorrect
Generated tests require developer review to ensure they test the right behaviour
Copilot cannot generate tests for any language other than JavaScript

Disable Copilot's security features and use the raw suggestion
Report the suggestion to GitHub and wait for a fix

Blocks all code changes until a security audit is completed
Emails the security team when a risky suggestion is accepted

The AI model itself
The developer who accepted and committed the suggestion
The organisation's legal department

q: Which term describes the responsible AI principle ensuring AI systems can be understood and scrutinised by stakeholders?

Accountability
Transparency
Security
exp: Transparency means AI systems and their decision-making can be understood and examined. It is distinct from accountability (who is responsible) and fairness (unbiased outputs).

q: A team discovers that Copilot suggestions for financial calculations contain systematic rounding errors. What responsible AI concept does this illustrate?
opts: Insufficient context
LLM hallucination and the need for human validation
Duplication filter interference
Insufficient GPU resources

q: Which two of the following reflect the principle of 'security' in responsible AI use of GitHub Copilot? (Select 2)

Assuming AI-generated code is secure because GitHub's filters are comprehensive
Using Copilot's security warning feature as one layer of a broader security practice
Deploying AI-generated code without penetration testing to save time

q: A developer uses Copilot to generate an image classification model. It performs poorly on under-represented demographic groups. Which responsible AI principle is most relevant?

Transparency
Fairness
Accountability

q: Which statement most accurately reflects the relationship between AI automation and human oversight in GitHub Copilot use?
opts: AI should handle all routine tasks autonomously to free developers from review burden
AI assists and augments developers, but human oversight and final decision-making remain essential
Copilot is reliable enough that oversight is optional for experienced developers
Oversight is only required for security-critical code, not general application code

q: Which of the following best illustrates the 'validate AI output' principle when using GitHub Copilot?

Executing a generated SQL query against the production database immediately to test it
Running the generated code through unit tests and code review before merging
Accepting suggestions only from trusted team members who use Copilot

q: Which two of the following best represent the principle of 'identifying potential harms' in responsible AI use of Copilot? (Select 2)

Assuming that all Copilot suggestions are safe because they are filtered
Identifying cases where AI suggestions may perpetuate biased outcomes in code logic
Trusting that GitHub's legal team has reviewed all potential AI harms

Because GitHub's terms of service prohibit use in safety-critical systems
Because Copilot's suggestions are always outdated for safety standards

It automatically connects to a live environment for real-data testing
It removes the need for a test framework
exp: Copilot can suggest assertions based on function signatures and expected behaviour, accelerating test writing — but the developer must review their correctness.

q: Which two of the following are valid use cases for GitHub Copilot in a security review workflow? (Select 2)
opts: Having Copilot suggest input validation code to prevent injection attacks
Using Copilot to automatically patch CVEs in production without review
Asking Copilot to review a function for common vulnerability patterns
Letting Copilot approve security exceptions in the audit log
exp: Copilot can suggest secure coding patterns and review code for vulnerabilities. Auto-patching production and approving audit exceptions require human decision-making.

q: Which of the following represents the correct approach when Copilot generates a security-relevant function (e.g. authentication logic)?
opts: Deploy it immediately since Copilot's filters ensure security
Use it as a starting point, then apply security-focused code review, static analysis, and penetration testing
Accept it only if the developer has Enterprise-level access
Disable Copilot for authentication modules as it cannot be trusted there
exp: Security-critical code generated by AI requires the full security review and testing stack. Copilot is a starting point — not a replacement for secure development practices.

q: In which scenario is Agent mode the LEAST appropriate choice?
opts: Refactoring a complex feature across 15 files
Asking a quick question about what a specific function does
Autonomously writing and running tests for a new module
Delegating a multi-step implementation task to AI
exp: Quick conversational questions are best handled by Ask mode. Agent mode's overhead is unnecessary for a simple Q&A.

q: A developer wants Copilot to suggest code in the style of the team's existing codebase. What is the most effective approach?
opts: Upgrade to Enterprise so Copilot can be fine-tuned on the codebase
Keep relevant files open as tabs so Copilot includes them in context
Disable Copilot and write the code manually
Use the /style command in Copilot Chat
exp: Keeping relevant files open as tabs provides Copilot with context about the codebase's style and patterns, improving the relevance of suggestions.

q: Which two activities are part of the GitHub Copilot Chat experience in the IDE? (Select 2)
opts: Asking Copilot to explain a selected block of code
Committing code directly from the Chat panel
Generating a refactored version of a function through chat
Deploying an application to GitHub Pages
exp: Copilot Chat supports code explanation and refactoring requests in the IDE. It does not commit code or deploy applications.

q: What is the primary use case for GitHub Copilot's 'Edit mode'?
opts: Exploring and learning about a codebase through Q&A
Making targeted code modifications with a before/after diff for developer approval
Planning a multi-file refactoring strategy
Autonomously completing an entire feature implementation
exp: Edit mode is designed for precise, targeted edits — the developer specifies what to change, Copilot suggests the edit with a diff preview, and the developer approves.

q: A developer uses Copilot on a mobile device. Which Copilot surface supports this?
opts: Only the desktop IDE extension
GitHub Copilot Mobile via the GitHub Mobile app
Copilot CLI on mobile
Copilot is not available on mobile devices
exp: GitHub Copilot Mobile is available through the GitHub Mobile app, extending AI assistance to mobile devices.

q: A developer opens Copilot Chat and types '/explain'. What does this do?
opts: Opens the Copilot documentation website
Triggers Copilot to explain the selected code or current context
Exports the chat history to a file
Resets the Copilot session
exp: /explain is a Copilot Chat slash command that triggers an explanation of selected code or the current code context.

q: What does the term 'Agent Session' refer to in GitHub Copilot?
opts: A scheduled background task that runs Copilot periodically
An interactive working session where Copilot Agent operates autonomously across files, tools, and actions until a task is complete
A shared session where multiple developers collaborate with the same Copilot context
A supervised mode where all Copilot actions require explicit approval
exp: An Agent Session is the interactive environment within which Agent mode operates — the AI can plan, write, test, and iterate across the codebase within that session.

q: What happens in an Agent mode session when the task exceeds the context window limit?
opts: Agent mode automatically upgrades the plan to Enterprise
Sub-agents can be used to distribute context across parallel tasks, managing the overall context load
The session terminates with an error
The developer must restart from scratch
exp: Agent mode uses Sub-agents to help manage context by delegating portions of work to separate agents, helping to work around context window limitations.

q: Which Copilot feature would most help a developer understand why a complex regular expression was written the way it was?
opts: Plan mode
Pull Request summaries
Copilot Chat — Ask mode with the regex selected
Agent mode
exp: Ask mode in Copilot Chat allows a developer to select the regex and ask for an explanation, receiving a plain-language breakdown of what it matches and why.

q: Which feature allows developers to share a consistent set of instructions and context with their whole team for a specific project?
opts: copilot-instructions.md
Copilot Spaces
Agent Sub-Sessions
Duplication filter policy
exp: Copilot Spaces allows teams to create shared environments with shared instructions, context, and knowledge, ensuring consistent AI-assisted experiences for the whole team.

q: A developer wants to reuse a specific prompt template across multiple Copilot Chat sessions for consistent test generation. What feature supports this?
opts: Agent sessions
Prompt files (.github/prompts/)
copilot-instructions.md
Copilot Spaces
exp: Prompt files (.github/prompts/) are reusable, shareable templates for specific tasks that can be invoked consistently across sessions.

q: What does 'Copilot Code Review' allow when configured by a Business plan admin?
opts: Automatic merging of approved pull requests
AI-generated review comments posted directly on pull requests as an automated reviewer
Blocking developers from committing code that Copilot flags
Generating test cases automatically from PR diffs
exp: Copilot Code Review posts automated AI-generated review comments on pull requests when configured as a reviewer. It does not auto-merge or block commits.

q: Which Copilot mode is best suited for making a targeted change to a single function while previewing the diff before applying?
opts: Ask mode
Edit mode
Plan mode
Agent mode
exp: Edit mode is designed for targeted, in-place code modifications with a diff preview. It is ideal for focused changes to specific functions or sections.

q: Which two of the following can a developer accomplish with GitHub Copilot CLI? (Select 2)
opts: Get a natural language explanation of a complex git command
Edit source code files directly from the terminal using Copilot
Generate a shell script to automate a file management task
Configure organisation-level Copilot policies from the terminal
exp: Copilot CLI supports command explanation and script/command generation. It does not directly edit source code files or configure org policies.

q: What type of tasks is GitHub Copilot CLI designed to assist with?
opts: IDE code completion only
Generating, explaining, and debugging shell commands and scripts in the terminal
Managing GitHub repository settings via command line
Running automated code reviews on pull requests
exp: Copilot CLI extends AI assistance to the terminal — it helps construct shell commands, explain existing commands, and generate scripts.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of GitHub Copilot CLI?
opts: Suggesting shell commands based on a natural language description
Explaining what a given shell command does
Generating and running Python notebooks interactively
Helping with git and gh commands interactively
exp: Copilot CLI focuses on terminal/shell commands and scripts. Generating Python notebooks interactively is not a CLI feature.

q: What is 'prompt injection' in the context of AI tools like GitHub Copilot?
opts: A technique for injecting SQL into database prompts
An attack where malicious content in code or documents attempts to manipulate Copilot's output in unintended ways
A method for injecting additional context into a prompt
A feature for inserting saved prompts into the chat window
exp: Prompt injection is a security concern where adversarial content (e.g. in code comments) attempts to hijack or manipulate an AI model's behaviour. It is a known LLM limitation.

q: Which two of the following represent ways GitHub Copilot can reduce developer toil (repetitive, low-value work)? (Select 2)
opts: Automatically generating boilerplate setup code for new projects
Making architectural decisions on behalf of the developer
Generating repetitive data transformation functions
Deciding the system design for a new service
exp: Boilerplate generation and repetitive function generation reduce toil. Architectural and design decisions require human judgment.

q: A developer generates a function with Copilot and then asks Copilot to generate tests for it in the same session. What context advantage does this provide?
opts: None — test generation always starts fresh with no context
Copilot can use the function's implementation from the session context to generate more targeted, accurate tests
Copilot will automatically run the tests and report results
The tests are guaranteed to achieve 100% line coverage
exp: Having the function implementation in the session context allows Copilot to generate tests that reflect the actual logic, parameters, and edge cases of that specific function.

q: Which Copilot plan allows an organisation to receive AI-powered code review on github.com as part of pull request workflows?
opts: Pro
Free
Business
Enterprise — it requires fine-tuned models
exp: Copilot Code Review as an organisation-level workflow feature on github.com requires Business or Enterprise plan.

q: Which two of the following represent correct uses of the copilot-instructions.md file? (Select 2)
opts: Defining the team's preferred coding style and conventions for Copilot to follow
Listing file paths to exclude from Copilot suggestions
Providing domain-specific context (e.g. 'this is a financial trading system') to improve suggestion relevance
Setting the organisation's plan tier for Copilot
exp: copilot-instructions.md is for coding conventions and domain context. File exclusions go in content exclusion settings, not this file.

q: Which of the following is the correct statement about the Copilot audit log and GDPR compliance?
opts: The audit log stores personal prompt data that must be deleted on request
The audit log records administrative events (not prompt content), and GitHub's data handling policies for Business/Enterprise are designed to support compliance frameworks
The audit log automatically anonymises all entries after 90 days
Organisations must export and manage the audit log themselves for GDPR purposes
exp: GitHub's data handling commitments for Business/Enterprise (no prompt retention, audit log of administrative events) are designed to help organisations meet compliance requirements including GDPR.

q: Which of the following describes a scenario where Copilot's Agent mode would use an MCP server?
opts: Fetching a suggestion from the underlying LLM
Connecting to an external project management tool (e.g. Jira) to read ticket details as part of a task
Running a content exclusion check on a local file
Posting an audit log event to the organisation admin
exp: MCP servers extend Agent mode with external tools. Connecting to Jira to read ticket details during a coding task is a typical MCP server use case.

q: An organisation wants to use the Copilot REST API to automatically provision access for new hires. Which plan is required, and what does the API allow?
opts: Pro — allows setting individual IDE preferences
Business or Enterprise — allows adding and removing Copilot seats programmatically
Free — allows read-only access to usage metrics
Enterprise — allows modifying the underlying LLM configuration
exp: The Copilot REST API for seat management (add/remove users) requires Business or Enterprise. This enables automation of onboarding/offboarding workflows.

q: A developer has been using GitHub Copilot for 6 months and starts accepting suggestions without review because they trust the tool. What risk does this behaviour introduce?
opts: It violates GitHub's terms of service
It increases the risk of undetected bugs, security vulnerabilities, and technical debt accumulating in the codebase
It will cause the Copilot subscription to be automatically downgraded
It reduces the developer's code quality metrics permanently
exp: Over-reliance on AI suggestions without review is a core responsible AI anti-pattern. Even experienced Copilot users must review suggestions — the tool can generate incorrect or insecure code.

q: What does 'post-processing' refer to in GitHub Copilot's output pipeline?
opts: Formatting the suggestion to match the developer's IDE theme
Applying additional filters (safety, duplication, security) to the raw LLM output before it is shown to the developer
Sending the suggestion to the audit log before display
Translating the suggestion to the developer's preferred language
exp: Post-processing applies safety, duplication, and policy filters to raw model output. This is a second layer of filtering after the model responds, before suggestions reach the IDE.

q: A developer generates a security-relevant function (authentication logic) with Copilot. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Deploy it immediately since Copilot's filters ensure security
Apply security-focused code review, static analysis, and penetration testing before deploying
Accept it only if the developer has Enterprise-level access
Disable Copilot for authentication modules as it cannot be trusted there
exp: Security-critical code requires the full security review stack. Copilot is a starting point — not a replacement for secure development practices.

q: A developer is unsatisfied with Copilot's suggestions and wants to improve them without changing the code. What is the most effective action?
opts: Restart the IDE
Refine the prompt with more specific instructions and relevant context
Downgrade to a lower Copilot plan
Disable and re-enable the Copilot extension
exp: Prompt quality directly drives suggestion quality. Refining the prompt with more specificity and context is the most effective way to improve results.

q: A developer is writing a function to parse a complex JSON schema. They have a sample JSON object in the file. How does Copilot use this to help?
opts: It uploads the JSON to a GitHub API for schema inference
It uses the sample JSON as context to generate a parser that handles the observed structure
It blocks suggestions until the full JSON schema is provided
It ignores data objects and only suggests code based on function signatures
exp: Copilot uses the sample JSON in context to infer the data structure and generate relevant parsing code.

q: An org admin enables Copilot for all members but sets content exclusions for files in a /secrets/ directory. A developer opens a file from /secrets/. What happens?
opts: Copilot suggests code as normal but adds a warning
No suggestions appear and Copilot does not use the file as context
The developer is asked to confirm they have permission to view the file
Copilot logs the access to the audit log and suggests code
exp: Content exclusions prevent Copilot from using excluded files as context and from generating suggestions within them. No warning or confirmation prompt is shown.

q: A developer wants to ensure Copilot Code Review is available on all their organisation's repositories. What must be configured?
opts: Enable it per repository in .github settings only
Configure Copilot Code Review policies at the organisation level
Upgrade to Enterprise — Code Review is not available on Business
Ask each developer to enable it in their IDE
exp: Copilot Code Review policies can be enabled at the organisation level on Business plans, making it available across all repositories in the org.

q: What is the purpose of GitHub Copilot usage metrics in an enterprise context?
opts: To monitor the content of developers' prompts for compliance
To help admins understand adoption rates, identify low-usage teams, and justify the Copilot subscription investment
To automatically revoke licences from inactive users
To measure developer productivity in lines of code generated
exp: Usage metrics help organisations track adoption and value — who is using Copilot, how often, and at what acceptance rate — supporting licence management and ROI decisions.

q: A developer uses Copilot on github.com to review a large PR. The PR modifies files in 20 locations. Which feature helps them understand the overall change quickly?
opts: Copilot CLI explain command
Copilot Pull Request Summaries
Content exclusion settings
Agent mode
exp: Pull Request Summaries generates an AI-written overview of the PR's changes, purpose, and impact — ideal for quickly understanding large or complex pull requests.

q: What is 'hallucination' in the context of GitHub Copilot and LLMs?
opts: A visual glitch in the IDE caused by the Copilot extension
When an LLM generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or fabricated information
When Copilot misidentifies the programming language
An audio notification from the IDE when a suggestion is ready
exp: Hallucination is the tendency of LLMs to generate confident, plausible-sounding output that is actually incorrect. It is a fundamental limitation requiring human validation.

q: A developer uses `/test` in Copilot Chat. What is the most likely function of this slash command?
opts: It runs the project's test suite
It asks Copilot to generate tests for the selected or current code
It opens the test results panel
It disables Copilot for test files
exp: /test is a Copilot Chat slash command that triggers test generation for the current code selection or file context.

q: Which two of the following correctly describe the proxy layer in GitHub Copilot's architecture? (Select 2)
opts: It sits between the developer's IDE and the AI model
It is installed locally on the developer's machine
It applies pre- and post-processing filters to prompts and suggestions
It stores all accepted suggestions for model retraining
exp: The proxy is GitHub-hosted (not local) and handles filtering of both incoming prompts and outgoing suggestions — a key architectural component.

q: Which statement about GitHub Copilot Free is true?
opts: It includes unlimited suggestions with no restrictions
It has monthly usage limits and does not include org-level policy controls
It is only available to GitHub employees
It requires a paid GitHub account to access
exp: Copilot Free has usage limits and is for individual developers only. It does not include Business/Enterprise features like org-level policies or audit logs.

q: An admin wants to use Copilot Code Review across the entire organisation. On which plan can they configure this as an org-wide policy?
opts: Pro only
Free only
Business or Enterprise
Enterprise only
exp: Copilot Code Review can be configured as an organisation-wide policy on Business or Enterprise plans.

q: Which of the following is the most accurate description of Copilot's impact on developer flow state?
opts: Copilot interrupts flow state by requiring constant review of suggestions
Copilot helps maintain flow by reducing interruptions for documentation lookups, boilerplate, and repetitive patterns — keeping developers in the editor
Copilot eliminates the need for developers to think about implementation details
Copilot only helps with flow when working in a new language
exp: By reducing the need to context-switch for documentation or boilerplate, Copilot helps developers stay in flow — a key developer productivity benefit.

q: A developer uses Copilot to identify edge cases for a sorting algorithm. What is Copilot's role?
opts: It runs the algorithm against all possible inputs automatically
It suggests potential edge cases (empty arrays, single elements, duplicates) based on the code context, which the developer then validates
It guarantees that all identified edge cases cover every possible failure mode
It deploys the test cases to a CI pipeline automatically
exp: Copilot suggests edge cases based on code analysis, but cannot guarantee completeness. The developer must validate and add any missed cases.

q: A developer wants Copilot to understand their organisation's internal framework conventions when generating code. They cannot use Enterprise fine-tuning. What is the most effective alternative?
opts: Send the conventions as an email to GitHub support
Add the conventions to .github/copilot-instructions.md so they are always included as context
Manually describe conventions in every prompt
Upgrade to Business plan
exp: copilot-instructions.md provides always-on repository-level context for Copilot Chat, making it the most practical way to inject framework conventions without Enterprise fine-tuning.

q: An organisation's CISO asks: 'Can we see which developers accepted Copilot suggestions in a sensitive file?' What is the correct answer?
opts: Yes — the audit log records all suggestion acceptances with file paths
Yes — the usage metrics dashboard shows file-level acceptance data
No — Copilot does not record which specific suggestions were accepted or which files they were in
No — only the developer's local IDE stores this information
exp: Copilot does not log which specific suggestions were accepted or which files they belonged to. Usage metrics are aggregated statistics; audit logs record administrative events only.

q: A developer uses Copilot to generate a complete CRUD API. After reviewing, they find the generated code is well-structured but uses a deprecated library. What is the best approach?
opts: Reject all generated code and write the CRUD API from scratch
Accept the generated structure and refactor the deprecated library usage manually, using Copilot to assist with the migration
Report the bug to GitHub and wait for a fix
Disable the duplication filter and regenerate
exp: AI-generated code is a starting point. Keeping the useful structure while fixing the deprecated dependency — with Copilot's help — is the optimal developer workflow.
